newsitem.title: CHINA: China banks urged to consider public flotation.
newsitem.headline: China banks urged to consider public flotation.

text.p: Chinese banks should consider new means of expanding their capital base, including the possible flotation of a proportion of shares in the public markets, a senior central bank official said on Monday.

Di Weiping, executive vice president of the People's Bank of China's Shanghai branch, said new joint stock company banks created in the past few years, such as the Pudong Development Bank and the Shanghai United City Bank, had proved successful.
The banks, while still state-owned, have none of the policy responsibilities of the major state banks, and more freedom to make decisions on a purely commercial basis.
Di said a suitable model for reform of some parts of the domestic banking sector could be the Shenzhen Development Bank.
The bank is the only publicly listed bank in China. It was launched in 1990 with 30 percent of its stock publicly tradeable, which was later raised to around 70 percent.
"We could perhaps move gradually in this direction," Di said. "It would remove a capital problem for some banks, and also help develop the stock markets."
The Shenzhen-based bank, created from the merger of six agricultural credit cooperatives in the late 1980s, last week reported an 81 percent rise in net profits for 1996.
"The government can set up some restrictions -- for instance 30 or 40 percent of the shares must be owned by institutional investors," Di said.
Di stressed there was no current plan for any other Chinese banks to list, but said he felt it was an avenue worth exploring to develop both the banking industry and the capital markets.
"If we move in that direction, it would resolve part of the problems for some of the banks. And also make the current stock exchanges develop in a more standardised way," he said.

"The Shenzhen Development Bank was an experiment, we could expand on it now. (Having part of the stock publicly traded) would strengthen the internal systems of the banks and help to make them more transparent," he added.
The use of convertible bonds by China's state-owned banks was another possibility worth considering, Di said.
Convertible bonds offered greater flexibility for the issuer in what type of equity is created on conversion, thereby making it easier to safeguard controls, Di said.
Shenzhen Development Bank, posted a net profit of 787.48 million yuan for 1996 against 435.13 million in 1995 under Chinese accounting standards.
Outstanding deposits, including foreign currency deposits, stood at 22.84 billion yuan at end-1996, up 45.6 percent from end-1995, the bank said in its annual report.
